opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key thing to understand is that industrial robots have been enormously successful precisely because factories are structured environments. On an automotive assembly line, everything is controlled: the part arrives at exactly the same position, the lighting is the same, the fixtures hold things in place to within a fraction of a millimeter. Under those conditions, a robot can repeat the same motion millions of times with incredible precision, and that's been true since the 1960s.

The challenge comes the moment you relax any of those constraints. If the lighting changes, if a part is slightly rotated, if a box is a little crushed, if a cable is draped differently than it was yesterday, the robot that was programmed for the exact scenario often just fails. And it fails in ways that seem almost absurd to us, because humans adapt to those variations effortlessly. We don't even notice them.

I like to frame this in terms of uncertainty. There's uncertainty in perception, because cameras and sensors are noisy, and things like transparent or shiny objects are really hard to see. There's uncertainty in control, because motors and joints aren't perfect. And there's uncertainty in physics: friction, mass distribution, how an object will slide or tip when you push it. These are extremely hard to model precisely. In a structured factory you engineer that uncertainty away. In a warehouse, a home, a hospital, or even a more flexible factory, you can't.

This is related to what's sometimes called Moravec's paradox: the things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, turned out to be relatively easy for computers, while the things a toddler does, like picking up an unfamiliar object, are remarkably hard for robots. Grasping a novel object in a cluttered bin is still an open research problem in many respects.

So a lot of the work in my lab and in the field has been about robustness: how do you design systems that perform reliably despite those variations? We've explored approaches like training on huge numbers of simulated examples with randomized conditions, so the system learns policies that hold up across a range of situations rather than one exact case. That's what underlay our Dex-Net work on grasping. More recently there's been a lot of excitement about large learned models, and I think they're genuinely promising, but I'd add a note of caution: robotics doesn't have the internet-scale data that language models had, so I think we'll need to combine learning with good old-fashioned engineering, physics, and careful modeling for some time.

And practically, I think the most realistic path is to accept that robots won't handle every variation, and design systems where they can recognize when they're uncertain and ask a human for help. That combination of automation and human oversight is, to me, where much of the near-term value lies.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it: industrial robots have been enormously successful for about sixty years, and the reason they work is that we engineered the environment around them. On a car assembly line, everything is fixed. The car body arrives at exactly the same position, the lighting is constant, the part the robot has to weld is always in the same place to within a fraction of a millimeter. The robot doesn't really perceive anything, it just replays a trajectory. That's why there are millions of them and they're very reliable.

The challenge comes when you take that robot out of the cage, or when the environment starts to drift. Even in a factory, a conveyor belt wears, a fixture gets bumped, the lights change over the day, a supplier sends slightly different parts. In a warehouse or a home it's far worse. Every object is different, it's sitting in a different pose, things are occluded, surfaces are shiny or transparent, and the physics of contact is genuinely hard to predict. I like to say that grasping is still unsolved. If I put a random object in front of a robot and ask it to pick it up and not drop it, the best systems are still well short of what a two-year-old can do.

So the core problem is uncertainty. Uncertainty in perception, where the sensors give you a noisy, partial picture of the world. Uncertainty in control, where the arm doesn't go exactly where you told it. And uncertainty in physics, where friction and mass and compliance are things you can't observe directly. Classical robotics handled this by eliminating uncertainty through engineering. The new approach is to try to make robots robust to it, through learning from large amounts of data, through better simulation, and through designs like soft grippers that are forgiving by nature.

I'm optimistic, but I'd caution against the narrative that this is about to be solved because of language models. Language models learned from the entire internet. There's no equivalent internet of robot manipulation data. What I think will actually happen is a hybrid, where we use learning where it helps, keep the classical geometry and physics where that's reliable, and in many cases keep a human in the loop for the hard cases. That's the realistic path for robots that have to work when the environment refuses to hold still.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental issue is uncertainty. In a factory, we’ve traditionally made robots reliable by controlling their environment very carefully. You put a part in a fixture so that it’s in exactly the same position every time, and then the robot can repeat the same motion with extraordinary precision.

But if the part shifts, or the lighting changes, or the material behaves a little differently, that motion may no longer work. The robot can be very precise and still do the wrong thing, because its assumptions about the world are no longer correct.

So the challenge is to move beyond simply repeating a motion toward sensing what’s happening, responding to changes, and recovering when something goes wrong. And sensing doesn’t eliminate uncertainty: cameras and other sensors give you imperfect information. You need a system that can act reliably despite that. That’s a much harder problem than getting a robot to perform a task once under carefully arranged conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that industrial robots are very good at repeating a motion, but that depends on the world being where they expect it to be. If you can fixture a part so that it arrives in exactly the same position and orientation every time, a robot can work very quickly and precisely. That’s a big part of why they’ve been so successful in factories.

But if the part shifts, or the lighting changes, or you introduce an object with a slightly different shape, the same motion may no longer work. The robot has to use sensing to figure out what’s changed and then adjust its actions. And the sensing itself is uncertain: a camera doesn’t give you perfect knowledge of where everything is.

So the problem is moving from repeatability in a carefully controlled environment to reliable behavior under variation. We can demonstrate a robot doing something once, but getting it to do that consistently, across all those changes, is a much harder engineering challenge.
